\part{System}

\chapter{About this manual} \label{s:about}

\section{Scope and audience}

This manual is the technical reference for the \AsicNameForUserGuide{} microcontroller. It is written for firmware developers and board designers, and it assumes familiarity with 32-bit microcontrollers, memory-mapped peripherals and the RISC-V instruction set. It describes the hardware as implemented: the address map, every peripheral and its registers, the interrupt fabric, the boot ROM and the processor core's configuration. The RISC-V specifications are normative for the instruction set and for the privileged architecture; where this manual restates them it does so only to say which parts are implemented and how. Where the implementation deviates from a specification, the deviation is stated where it applies.

Everything in this manual is generated from one chip configuration, the same one that produces the RTL, the C headers and the linker scripts (Section~\ref{ss:chipConfig}), so a value printed here is the value built.

\section{Organisation of this manual}

\begin{description}[style=nextline, leftmargin=0pt, itemsep=2pt]
	\item[Part I, System] What is on the chip, its package and pins, the address map, the multi-core architecture, and reset, clocks and power. Read this part first.
	\item[Part II, Processor] The VestaRV core: its instruction set, control and status registers, privileged architecture, interrupts and exceptions, instruction timing, and the debug system.
	\item[Part III, Peripherals] One chapter per peripheral, each with a functional description, a programming sequence, usage notes and the complete register description.
	\item[Part IV, Analog front end] The mixed-signal front end and its characterisation.
	\item[Part V, Boot ROM and software] The ROM monitor and the boot image format the boot ROM loads.
	\item[Appendices] Getting started and software development, the register index, errata, and the revision history of this document.
\end{description}

\section{Conventions} \label{ss:conventions}

\begin{description}[style=nextline, leftmargin=0pt, itemsep=2pt]
	\item[Numbers] Hexadecimal numbers carry the prefix \texttt{0x} (\texttt{0x4600}); binary numbers carry the prefix \texttt{0b} (\texttt{0b101}); decimal numbers have no prefix. A value of the form \texttt{0x8000 + 4n} is an address formula in which $n$ is the array index.
	\item[Units] Capacities are binary: 1 KiB is 1024 bytes. Rates and frequencies are decimal: 115,200 baud, 24 MHz. A word is 32 bits, a half-word 16 bits and a byte 8 bits.
	\item[Registers and fields] A register is named by its peripheral template and register name, and a field by the dotted form \texttt{PERIPHERAL.\allowbreak REGISTER.\allowbreak FIELD}, for example \register{TIMx.TIMxCR.TEN}. In prose, register names are the template form (\register{PxIN}, \register{TIMxCR}), where \texttt{x} stands for the instance number; the instance form (\register{P0IN}, \register{TIM0CR}) appears only in the per-instance address tables and in the generated headers.
	\item[Bit ranges] Bits are numbered from 0 at the least significant end. A range is written \texttt{[h:l]} with the high bit first; \texttt{[7:4]} is four bits. A single bit is written \texttt{[n]}.
	\item[Set and clear] A bit is set when it holds 1 and cleared when it holds 0. Asserted means the active level of a signal, whatever its polarity; an active-low pin is named with a trailing \texttt{N} (\pin{RESETN}).
	\item[Reserved] A reserved bit reads as zero and must be written as zero. No exception is raised by an access to a reserved bit or to a reserved register offset inside a peripheral's window.
	\item[Register width] Every register is described at its natural width, 8 or 32 bits, and every register occupies one 4-byte slot at a 4-byte aligned offset regardless of its width; the unused upper bytes of an 8-bit register are reserved.
	\item[Narrow accesses] The bus carries four byte-lane write strobes, so a byte or half-word store reaches the peripheral with only the addressed lanes asserted. Reads always return the full word of the addressed slot. Whether a partial write is honoured is a property of the register: an 8-bit register lives in byte lane 0, and a register described as requiring a full-word write commits only stores that assert lane 0.
\end{description}

\section{The anatomy of a register description} \label{ss:anatomy}

Every register in Part~III is described in the same layout. The example below is a fictitious register, \register{DUMMY.DUMMYCR}, chosen to show every element once; the callouts after it name each element.

\begin{center}
\begin{minipage}{0.96\linewidth}
\subsection*{DUMMYxCR: Dummy control register}
\noindent \textbf{Offset} \texttt{0x04} \quad \textbf{Reset} \texttt{0x00000000} \quad \textbf{Width} 32

\noindent Controls the dummy function. One or two sentences say what the register is for and point to the functional section that explains it.

\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{l l l l X}
\hline \textbf{Bits} & \textbf{Field} & \textbf{Type} & \textbf{Reset} & \textbf{Description} \\ \hline
\texttt{[31:8]} & - & - & - & Reserved. Reads zero; write zero. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{[7:4]} & \texttt{DIV} & \texttt{rw} & \texttt{0x0} & Clock divider. The dummy clock is the source divided by $2^{\mathtt{DIV}}$. \\
\texttt{[3:2]} & \texttt{MODE} & \texttt{rw} & \texttt{0b00} & Operating mode. \newline \texttt{0b00} = \texttt{DMODE\_OFF}: the function is off. \newline \texttt{0b01} = \texttt{DMODE\_ONCE}: one operation, then off. \newline \texttt{0b10} = \texttt{DMODE\_CONT}: continuous. \newline \texttt{0b11} = reserved. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{[1]} & \texttt{DIF} & \texttt{rw1} & \texttt{0} & Done interrupt flag. Set by hardware when an operation completes; write 1 to clear. \\
\texttt{[0]} & \texttt{DEN} & \texttt{rw} & \texttt{0} & Enable. 0 = disabled, 1 = enabled. Write this bit last. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}
\end{minipage}
\end{center}

\begin{description}[style=nextline, leftmargin=0pt, itemsep=1pt]
	\item[Heading] The register's template name and a short title. The heading appears in the chapter's own register list, not in the main table of contents. The \texttt{x} in the name is the instance number.
	\item[Offset, Reset, Width] The byte offset from the instance base address (the base addresses are in the chapter's instance table), the reset value of the whole register, and its width in bits.
	\item[Summary sentence] What the register is for, in one to three sentences, with a pointer to the functional description for anything longer.
	\item[Field rows] One row per field, most significant first, every bit covered. \textbf{Bits} is the range, \textbf{Field} the name used in prose and in the generated headers (with the peripheral's field prefix), \textbf{Type} the access type of Table~\ref{t:access-types}, \textbf{Reset} the field's reset value at the field's width.
	\item[Enumerated values] Listed inside the description cell as \texttt{value} = \texttt{SYMBOL}: meaning. The symbol is the macro name in the generated header. Values are binary for fields of four bits or fewer and hexadecimal for wider fields.
	\item[Reserved runs] Consecutive reserved bits are collapsed into one row whose field, type and reset are a dash.
\end{description}

\section{Callouts} \label{ss:callouts}

Two kinds of callout appear in this manual, and only two. A \emph{Note} is advisory: it adds context or a recommendation, and nothing breaks if it is skipped. A \emph{Caution} states a constraint the hardware enforces: ignoring it causes a wrong result, a hang, or lost data.

\begin{Note}
A note looks like this. It is at most a few sentences long.
\end{Note}

\begin{Caution}
A caution looks like this. Software must satisfy the condition it states, because the hardware does not check it.
\end{Caution}

\section{Glossary of terms and abbreviations} \label{ss:glossary}

\begin{acronym}[IRQROUTER]
	\acro{ABI}{Application binary interface: the register-usage and calling convention of Table~\ref{t:cpu-registers}.}
	\acro{AF}{Alternate function: a peripheral signal a GPIO pin can carry instead of its plain I/O function; a pin has up to eight AF planes.}
	\acro{AFE}{Analog front end: the mixed-signal circuitry of Part~IV.}
	\acro{CLINT}{Core-local interruptor: the peripheral that provides each hart's software interrupt and timer interrupt.}
	\acro{CPI}{Cycles per instruction.}
	\acro{CRC}{Cyclic redundancy check.}
	\acro{CSR}{Control and status register: a register inside the processor core reached by the \asminline{csr*} instructions.}
	\acro{DM}{Debug module: the on-chip block that halts, resumes and inspects harts on behalf of an external debugger.}
	\acro{DMI}{Debug module interface: the register bus between the debug transport module and the debug module.}
	\acro{DTM}{Debug transport module: the JTAG-side block that converts scans into DMI accesses.}
	\acro{EIS}{Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy: the swept-frequency impedance measurement the analog front end performs.}
	\acro{GPIO}{General-purpose input and output.}
	\acro{hart}{Hardware thread: one RISC-V execution context. Every hart on this chip is a separate core with its own TCM.}
	\acro{I2C}[I\textsuperscript{2}C]{Inter-integrated circuit: the two-wire serial bus.}
	\acro{IPI}{Inter-processor interrupt: a CLINT software interrupt sent from one hart to another.}
	\acro{IRQROUTER}{Interrupt router: the peripheral that routes every interrupt source to any hart and provides the claim and complete registers.}
	\acro{ISA}{Instruction set architecture.}
	\acro{ISR}{Interrupt service routine.}
	\acro{IVT}{Interrupt vector table: the table of jump instructions at the base of each hart's TCM.}
	\acro{JTAG}{The IEEE 1149.1 test access port over which the debug transport operates.}
	\acro{MCU}{Microcontroller unit.}
	\acro{MTCMOS}{Multi-threshold CMOS power gating: the header switches that cut the supply of a hart tile.}
	\acro{MUTEX}{Hardware mutual-exclusion bank: the peripheral that provides atomically claimable locks.}
	\acro{NFC}{Near-field communication: the peripheral that reads a 13.56 MHz tag interface and, on a field-powered board, supplies the chip.}
	\acro{NPU}{Neural processing unit: the fixed-point matrix accelerator.}
	\acro{PGOOD}{Power good: the supply-supervisor input that releases the boot gate on a field-powered board.}
	\acro{PMP}{Physical memory protection: the RISC-V machine-mode memory protection unit, a configuration option.}
	\acro{POC}{Power-on control: the input of the I/O pad ring that holds the pads in a safe state while the I/O supply rises. It is not a boot strap.}
	\acro{POR}{Power-on reset.}
	\acro{PWRCTRL}{Power controller: the peripheral that gates hart tiles and holds the boot gate.}
	\acro{QSPI}{Quad serial peripheral interface: a four-data-line SPI variant, a configuration option.}
	\acro{ROM}{Read-only memory: the boot ROM at address \texttt{\RomStartAddress}.}
	\acro{SPI}{Serial peripheral interface.}
	\acro{TCM}{Tightly coupled memory: the private RAM of one hart, \TcmSizeKiB{} KiB at \texttt{\RamStartAddress}, reached without arbitration.}
	\acro{TRNG}{True random number generator, a configuration option.}
	\acro{UART}{Universal asynchronous receiver and transmitter.}
	\acro{W1C}{Write one to clear: a flag bit that is cleared by writing 1 to it (access type \texttt{rw1}).}
	\acro{WARL}{Write any, read legal: a CSR field that accepts any written value and reads back a legal one.}
	\acro{XIP}{Execute in place: fetching instructions directly from the external SPI flash through the extended-flash window.}
\end{acronym}

\chapter{Overview} \label{s:config}
The \AsicNameForUserGuide{} microcontroller (MCU) is a \NumHartsWord-hart multiprocessor built from \NumHartsWord{} identical VestaRV cores, a 32-bit RISC-V processor, together with a boot ROM that contains the boot loader and a ROM monitor, a private tightly coupled memory (TCM) per hart, an arbitrated shared memory window for inter-hart communication, and the peripherals listed below. The multi-core architecture is described in Chapter~\ref{s:multicore}, and Figure~\ref{fig:chip-system-flat-diagram} shows the top-level organisation of this configuration.

\section{Chip configuration} \label{ss:chipConfig}

This document, the memory-map headers, the linker scripts, and the drop-in RTL are all generated from one chip configuration by \texttt{make chip}. The configuration is a small JSON document (every key optional; a missing key keeps the \AsicNameForUserGuide{} default) passed as \texttt{make chip CONFIG=config.json}; an interactive front end for producing it ships with the generator (\texttt{docs/chip\_configurator.html}). Table~\ref{t:chip-config} lists every configuration knob together with the value used to build this document, Table~\ref{t:chip-config-derived} lists the geometry derived from those knobs, and Table~\ref{t:hart-class-isa} lists the ISA of each hart class this build emitted. The resolved configuration is also written to \texttt{config/ChipConfig.resolved.json} at every build, and \texttt{make verify [CONFIG=config.json]} proves a configuration by staging the generated RTL into a behavioural simulation environment and running the multi-core boot and ISA smoke suite against it. The core peripheral set and the pad ring are not configuration knobs; they are fixed template content, and the pad ring (Chapter~\ref{s:pinsConfig}) is derived from the generator's package model. The second-instance peripherals (\peripheral{UART1}, \peripheral{SPI1}, \peripheral{TIMER1}, \peripheral{I2C1}) and the \peripheral{NPU} are individually droppable through the \texttt{peripherals} section: a dropped instance's register window reads zero, its interrupt vectors are reserved (the numbering is frozen), and its pins revert to plain GPIO.

\section{GPIO pins and alternate functions}

Most of the digital I/O pins are GPIO pins. A GPIO pin is in either primary (GPIO) mode or alternate function (peripheral) mode; see the \peripheral{GPIOx} chapter (Chapter~\ref{peripheralGPIOx}). Table~\ref{t:gpio-pins} lists every GPIO pin with its primary function, its reset-selected alternate function (AF0), and the reset state of its \register{PxSEL}, \register{PxOUT}, \register{PxDIR}, and \register{PxREN} bits. The remaining alternate functions each pin can select (AF1 to AF7) are in the alternate-function matrix, Table~\ref{t:gpio-afs}.

\input{include/GpioPinsConfigurationTable.tex}

When a pin is in alternate function mode (its \register{PxSEL} bit is 1), its 3-bit \register{PxAFS} field selects which of up to eight alternate functions (AF0 to AF7) drives the pad. Table~\ref{t:gpio-afs} lists, for every GPIO pin, the function selected by each \register{PxAFS} value. Plane 0 is the pin's AF0 function and is the reset selection; planes marked \textbf{Hi-Z} have no function assigned for that pin and configure the pad as a high-impedance input. The superscript on each function denotes its direction (\textsuperscript{\scriptsize in} input, \textsuperscript{\scriptsize out} output, \textsuperscript{\scriptsize io} bidirectional), and a \textsuperscript{$\dagger$} marks each pin's reset plane (its \register{PxAFS} reset value). While a pin is in primary mode the selected plane has no effect on the pad, but it still routes relocatable peripheral inputs (Chapter~\ref{peripheralGPIOx}).

\input{include/GpioAltFunctionMatrixTable.tex}

\chapter{Memory map} \label{s:addressSpace}

% Generated, configuration-driven address-space column (make chip). Placement is
% [!ht] because the column is this chapter's subject and the prose walks it. The
% caption is written to both polarities: the aperture band exists only where the
% configuration has an orchestrator, hence the \iforchpresent sentence below.
\begin{figure}[!ht]
	\centering
	% Natural size: the column is drawn to fit, and its labels are 8 pt.
	\input{include/AddressSpaceDiagram.tex}
	\caption[{\AsicNameForUserGuide{} address space: one column for all \NumHartsWord{} harts}]{\AsicNameForUserGuide{} address space: one gapless 32-bit column, drawn once for all \NumHartsWord{} harts; grey rows are unmapped and read zero.}
	\label{fig:address-space}
\end{figure}

The 32-bit memory bus is a single von Neumann address space: the ROM, the RAMs and the memory-mapped peripheral registers are all reached through one bus, and a pointer can address any of them. An access to an unmapped address reads zero, and a write to one is ignored; no bus error is raised.

The ROM holds the boot loader and the ROM monitor and is read-only. Each RAM can be read and written and may hold both code and data. The chip carries no on-die non-volatile memory: it boots from an external SPI flash device, and hart 0, and only hart 0, can additionally read that flash directly, and execute in place from it, through the extended-flash window at \texttt{\FlashBaseAddress} and above (the last region in Figure~\ref{fig:address-space}; see Section~\ref{ss:spi-flash-xip}). At reset every hart fetches from the boot ROM at \texttt{\RomStartAddress} and dispatches on its hart ID: hart 0 copies the application image out of the flash into memory and enters it, and the remaining harts park until hart 0 loads and launches them (Section~\ref{ss:multicore-boot}). Each RAM and ROM block can be individually powered off and on through the \peripheral{SYSTEM} peripheral; a block that is powered off draws less static power, does not respond, and a RAM loses its contents.

Figure~\ref{fig:address-space} is a single address column drawn for all \NumHartsWord{} harts, and its braces name who reaches each region. Everything below \texttt{\FlashBaseAddress} other than the private band is the shared window: every hart reaches it through the arbiter, and all \NumHartsWord{} harts see the same memory there (Chapter~\ref{s:multicore}). The private band is the exception: at those addresses a hart reaches its own TCM instead of the shared bus, so the same address names a different \TcmSizeKiB{} KiB of RAM in each hart, and no hart can reach another's directly.

Table~\ref{t:address-map} is the same column as a table, one row per decoded region with its access attributes; the register-level index of every peripheral is Appendix~\ref{s:regMemMap}.
\IfFileExists{include/AddressSpaceTable.tex}{\input{include/AddressSpaceTable.tex}}{}
\iforchpresent
% Aperture stride: 0x4000 (16 KiB) per hart regardless of TCM size, from
% _tcmApertureSize in python/generate.py and the s_addr(15:12) decode in
% hdl/common/hart_tile.vhd. A TCM smaller than the stride mirrors inside its
% aperture. The generator exports no define for the stride, so the literal is here.
The TCM apertures are the one sanctioned way across that line: hart \OrchHartIndex, the orchestrator, reads hart $h$'s private TCM through the aperture at \texttt{\FirstTcmWindowAddress}${} + h \times{}$\texttt{0x4000}. The aperture stride is 16 KiB whatever the TCM size, so a \TcmSizeKiB{} KiB TCM is mirrored inside its aperture. The apertures are read-only, and any other hart reading them gets zeros (Chapter~\ref{s:multicore}).
\fi
The extended-flash window is likewise hart 0's alone; the other harts' accesses in that range read zeros without stalling.

The interrupt vector table (IVT) begins at \texttt{\VectorsStartAddress}, the base of each hart's TCM, and holds one 4-byte jump instruction per vector (Chapter~\ref{s:interrupts}).

Peripheral registers occupy one 4-byte slot each, at 4-byte aligned offsets from the instance base address, whatever their width. The \peripheral{GPIOx} port registers are 8 bits wide, one bit per pin, and occupy byte lane 0 of their slot; a 32-bit register uses the whole slot. The register index in Appendix~\ref{s:regMemMap} gives the width of every register.

A read of a register that the peripheral's own clock domain writes, a status word or a receive buffer, returns a value up to two bus-clock edges older than the access, because the peripheral carries such a word into the bus clock through a synchroniser rather than sampling it on the select; the value is always a coherent snapshot of one register taken at one edge, a transfer launched by a write is already visible in that peripheral's busy bit on the next access, and a write-1-to-clear flag reads back cleared on the next access.

\chapter{Reset, clocks and power} \label{s:startup}

\section{Reset}

The chip is held in reset while the \pin{RESETN} pin is low and leaves reset when it is released high. A power-on reset circuit asserts the internal reset while the core supply rises from zero and releases it once the supply has reached its operating level; the chip is in reset whenever either \pin{RESETN} or the power-on reset is asserted. In reset, every memory-mapped register and every core state register is at its reset value. The \pin{RESETN} input has an internal pull-up and may be left unconnected.

Every hart leaves reset fetching from the boot ROM at \texttt{\RomStartAddress}. Hart 0 runs the boot loader; harts 1 to \MaxHartIndex{} park in the ROM until hart 0 releases them through the boot mailboxes in shared RAM (Section~\ref{ss:multicore-boot}). The \peripheral{PWRCTRL} boot gate can hold every hart in reset until a supply supervisor reports power good; see Section~\ref{s:powerdomains} and Chapter~\ref{peripheralPWRCTRL}.

\section{Boot mode selection} \label{ss:bootmode}

% The strap is GPIO port 0 pin 7 (package pin "P0.7(BOOT)"), read by the boot ROM
% through P0IN with mask 0x80: software/bootrom_mp/src/start.S (check_boot_mode) and
% software/commune/include/myshkin.h (GPIO0_BOOT_MASK). There is no dedicated BOOT pad.
Hart 0's boot loader samples one strap after reset: GPIO pin \pin{P0.7}, marked \pin{BOOT} in Table~\ref{t:gpio-pins}. The pin is read once, through \register{P0IN}, after the boot loader has configured the \peripheral{SPI0} pins; it is an ordinary GPIO pin at every other time. Table~\ref{t:boot-modes} gives the two modes.

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l l X}
\caption{Boot mode selected by the \pin{P0.7} strap.} \label{t:boot-modes} \\
\hline \textbf{\pin{P0.7} at reset} & \textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Behaviour} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{\pin{P0.7} at reset} & \textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Behaviour} \\ \hline \endhead
Low & ROM monitor & Hart 0 runs the interactive ROM monitor over \peripheral{UART0} at 115,200 baud (Chapter~\ref{s:forth}). \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} High & SPI flash & Hart 0 reads the boot image from the SPI flash on \peripheral{SPI0}, copies its segments into RAM and enters it (Chapter~\ref{s:programming}). \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

On a field-powered board the harvested-boot strap sampled by \peripheral{PWRCTRL} (\register{PWRSTS}) takes precedence: when it reads 1, hart 0 takes the harvested-boot path described in Chapter~\ref{peripheralPWRCTRL} before the \pin{P0.7} strap is consulted.

\begin{Note}
The boot ROM reprograms the clock system during boot, so the SMCLK source at application entry is a boot-ROM implementation detail and may be the slow LFXT source. An application that uses an SMCLK-domain peripheral (a UART, SPI, I\textsuperscript{2}C or a timer clock-source switch) selects its SMCLK source in the \peripheral{SYSTEM} peripheral first (Section~\ref{ss:clocks}).
\end{Note}

\part{Processor}

\chapter{VestaRV core} \label{s:cpu-instructions}

Every hart of the \AsicNameForUserGuide{} MCU is a VestaRV core, a 32-bit RISC-V processor with a single unified instruction and data bus. This chapter states what the core implements: its instruction set, its register conventions, its hart identities and its control and status registers. The RISC-V specifications named in Section~\ref{ss:related} are normative for the instructions and registers themselves and are not restated here.

\section{Instruction set} \label{ss:isa}

The ISA string of this build, the \texttt{-march} value the toolchain is given, is listed under \emph{ISA string} in Table~\ref{t:chip-config-derived}\ifdefined\IsaString{} and is \texttt{\IsaString}\fi. The same information is available at run time in the read-only \register{misa} register (Section~\ref{ss:csrs}). The extensions the core family implements are listed below with the configuration knob that selects each; which ones are present in this build is exactly what the ISA string says.

\begin{itemize}[itemsep=1pt]
	\item \textbf{RV32I}, the base integer instruction set: 32 registers of 32 bits, integer arithmetic, logic, shifts, comparisons, loads and stores of bytes, half-words and words, branches and jumps. Always present.
	\item \textbf{M} (\texttt{isa.mul}, \texttt{isa.div}): hardware multiply, divide and remainder, signed and unsigned. Multiply is single-cycle; divide is iterative (Chapter~\ref{s:cpi}).
	\item \textbf{A} (\texttt{isa.atomics}): load-reserved and store-conditional, and the atomic read-modify-write operations on 32-bit words. An atomic operation holds the shared-window arbiter grant across its whole read-modify-write pair, so it is atomic with respect to every hart (Section~\ref{ss:multicore-sync}).
	\item \textbf{C} (\texttt{isa.compressed}): 16-bit encodings of the most common instructions. Code built with it is substantially smaller; its fetch-alignment cost is measured in Section~\ref{ss:cpi-align}.
	\item \textbf{Zba, Zbb, Zbc, Zbs} (\texttt{isa.bitmanip}): address generation (shift-and-add), basic bit manipulation (count, min and max, rotate, sign and zero extension, byte reversal), carry-less multiplication, and single-bit set, clear, invert and extract.
	\item \textbf{Zicsr}: the CSR access instructions. Always present.
	\item \textbf{Zicntr}: the \register{cycle} and \register{instret} counters, readable from the user views. Always present; \register{time} is not implemented (Section~\ref{ss:csrs}).
\end{itemize}

An instruction of an extension that is not configured into the build raises an illegal-instruction exception; what happens next depends on the trap delivery mode (Section~\ref{ss:csr-unimplemented}).

Three instructions are specific to this core and are used by the runtime: \asminline{retirq} returns from a legacy-mode interrupt (Chapter~\ref{s:interrupts}), \asminline{sleep} gates the hart's clock until an interrupt arrives (Section~\ref{ss:sleep}), and \asminline{wake} is its counterpart. Their encodings are in the generated \texttt{periph.S}.

\section{Registers and calling convention} \label{ss:abi}

The 32 general-purpose registers and their roles under the standard RISC-V calling convention (the \texttt{ilp32} ABI) are listed in Table~\ref{t:cpu-registers}. The compiler follows this convention, so hand-written assembly that follows it is drop-in compatible with compiled code. A register whose saver is the caller may be overwritten by any function call; a register whose saver is the callee is preserved across calls.

\section{Hart identities} \label{ss:hartids}

Each hart reads its own identity in \register{mhartid}: \texttt{0} to \texttt{\MaxHartIndex}. The boot ROM dispatches on it (Section~\ref{ss:multicore-boot}), and it selects the hart's own \peripheral{CLINT} and \peripheral{IRQROUTER} rows.\iforchpresent{} Hart \OrchHartIndex{} is the orchestrator: it is always powered, it runs the boot loader and the ROM monitor, and it alone reaches the TCM apertures and the extended-flash window (Chapter~\ref{s:multicore}).\fi

\subsection{Unimplemented CSRs and illegal accesses} \label{ss:csr-unimplemented}

% Source of the rules below: hdl/common/vesta/maindec.vhd (csr_addr_valid,
% csr_ro_denied, dbg_csr_denied, u_csr_denied) and hdl/common/vesta/csr_unit.vhd.
A CSR instruction naming a register that is not in Tables~\ref{t:csr-always} and~\ref{t:csr-optional} for this build is an illegal instruction (exception code 2). In particular \register{time} and \register{timeh} (\texttt{0xC01}, \texttt{0xC81}) are not implemented, because no real-time source is wired to the core; use \register{cycle} and the known MCLK frequency instead. Two further rules apply in every configuration: a CSR instruction in a write form (any form other than a pure read with \asminline{x0} as the source) aimed at the read-only quadrant (\texttt{0xC00} to \texttt{0xFFF}) is illegal even when the register exists, and an access to the debug CSRs outside debug mode is illegal. A write to a WARL register listed as hard-wired (\register{misa}, \register{mip}, \register{mstatush}, \register{mcountinhibit}, the \register{mhpm*} ranges) is not illegal; it is accepted and ignored. An illegal CSR instruction commits nothing: no register, memory or CSR is changed.

What an illegal instruction does next depends on the trap delivery mode of Chapter~\ref{s:privarch}. In the legacy mode, which every configuration selects at reset, there is no recoverable exception: the hart enters a terminal trap state and retires no further instruction until reset. In the standard mode, available where \texttt{priv.trapCsr} is configured and selected by clearing \register{mtrapctl}.\bitfield{LEGACY}, the hart traps to \register{mtvec} with \register{mcause} = 2 and \register{mtval} holding the faulting encoding.

\begin{Caution}
The \asminline{unimp} pseudo-instruction assembles to a CSR write to \register{cycle} (\texttt{0xC0001073}), which is exactly the read-only-quadrant write described above. Reaching an \asminline{unimp} in legacy delivery mode halts the hart until reset.
\end{Caution}

\chapter{Interrupts and exceptions} \label{s:interrupts}

The VestaRV CPU implements an interrupt system with \VectorsCount{} interrupt vectors, numbered 0 to \TopVector, whose sources are enumerated in Table~\ref{t:interrupt-vectors}. The numbering is frozen: a vector belongs to the block that owns it whether or not this configuration instantiates that block, so vectors whose block is absent are reserved and counted with the rest rather than shifting the ones above them. Two of the \VectorsCount{} are the \peripheral{CLINT} pair (\ClintMsipVector, the software or inter-processor interrupt; \ClintMtipVector, the timer interrupt) added for multi-core operation; the other \RoutedVectorsCount{} sit on the \peripheral{IRQROUTER} side of the fabric: the peripheral and system sources, the reserved slots frozen among them, and \texttt{meip}'s own slot. Each hart takes three interrupt lines: its own \peripheral{CLINT} software and timer interrupts (vectors \ClintMsipVector{} and \ClintMtipVector, hardwired enabled, delivered on dedicated per-hart wires) and the external interrupt \texttt{meip} (vector \MeipVector, a slot of its own that no source pends on), which delivers all peripheral and system sources through the \peripheral{IRQROUTER}'s claim and complete mechanism: the vector-\MeipVector{} handler reads the router's \register{CLAIM} register to discover and claim the pending source, dispatches on the returned vector number, and writes it back to complete (Chapter~\ref{peripheralIRQROUTER}). Which sources reach which hart is programmed per hart in the router's routing rows, identical for every hart, hart 0 included. All peripheral sources are masked at reset and must be routed in software before use; source priority is fixed (the lowest pending vector number is claimed first). A peripheral must additionally be configured to generate its interrupt at the peripheral level.

% The vector table itself is generated (include/InterruptsTable_man.tex ->
% InterruptsTable.tex): one row per vector, reserved rows included.
\input{include/InterruptsTable_man.tex}

Figure~\ref{fig:irq-fabric-diagram}, in the \peripheral{IRQROUTER} chapter (Chapter~\ref{peripheralIRQROUTER}), draws the whole fabric in one view: the source population of Table~\ref{t:interrupt-vectors} collapsed by type, the \peripheral{IRQROUTER} as the spine every one of those sources terminates in, and the \NumHartsWord{} harts with the three lines each of them takes. It shows the one asymmetry: \texttt{meip} arrives from the router, and \texttt{msip} and \texttt{mtip} do not go near it.

\section{Exceptions}

In the legacy trap delivery mode selected at reset there is no recoverable exception: an illegal instruction, including an access to an unimplemented CSR, puts the hart into a terminal trap state (Section~\ref{ss:csr-unimplemented}). Where the standard delivery mode is configured and selected, exceptions vector through \register{mtvec} with the \register{mcause} codes of Table~\ref{t:priv-causes} in Chapter~\ref{s:privarch}. Table~\ref{t:cpu-exceptions} lists the causes that originate inside the hart rather than on a numbered vector.
\IfFileExists{include/CpuExceptionsTable.tex}{\input{include/CpuExceptionsTable.tex}}{}

\section{Interrupt vector table}

The interrupt vector table (IVT) is located at the base of each hart's TCM, beginning at address \texttt{\VectorsStartAddress}. Unlike a pointer-based vector table, the VestaRV IVT contains direct jump instructions to the interrupt service routines (ISRs): each entry is a 4-byte RISC-V jump instruction (for example \asminline{j handler}) that vectors execution immediately to the corresponding ISR when an interrupt occurs. This eliminates the indirection of loading a function pointer and gives a deterministic, low-latency interrupt response.

The hardware does not mandate a specific IVT content, so software populates the IVT with jump instructions during initialisation. The generated linker scripts and startup code place the IVT at the beginning of the TCM, and the generated header files provide macros for ISR placement and IVT entry configuration.

\section{Interrupt entry, exit and recursion}

When an interrupt is taken, the hardware saves a minimal context: it pushes the return program counter (one 32-bit word) onto the stack at $\mathtt{sp}-4$, decrements \asminline{sp} by 4, and vectors execution through the IVT entry for the interrupt. No other state is saved by hardware. Software is responsible for saving and restoring every general-purpose register the ISR uses. The generated runtime provides an interrupt entry wrapper (in the startup code) that saves the general-purpose registers on the stack (about 120 bytes per interrupt level), calls the C-level handler, restores the registers, and returns with the \asminline{retirq} instruction, so C-coded ISRs need no special handling. Hand-written assembly ISRs must perform the equivalent save and restore themselves. Executing \asminline{retirq} pops the hardware-saved program counter, increments \asminline{sp} by 4, and resumes execution at the interrupted location.

\begin{Caution}
Because the first thing interrupt entry does is a store at $\mathtt{sp}-4$, the stack pointer must point at valid, writable private memory before interrupts are enabled. This applies to every hart: a freshly released tile hart must load its stack pointer before unmasking interrupts or going to sleep (Chapter~\ref{s:multicore}).
\end{Caution}

Interrupt handling is non-recursive: a running ISR is never preempted, and further pending interrupts (including a pending \peripheral{CLINT} interrupt during a vector-\MeipVector{} service) are taken after the current ISR returns. Stack allocation must cover one interrupt level: the 4-byte hardware-saved return address plus the handler's register frame (about 120 bytes for the runtime wrapper) and the ISR's local variables. Source arbitration happens in the \peripheral{IRQROUTER}; the core itself has no priority tiers.

\section{Sleep mode and interrupt wake-up}

If an interrupt occurs while the CPU is in sleep mode, the processor wakes from sleep and services the interrupt. On execution of the \asminline{retirq} instruction, the CPU returns to sleep mode unless the ISR or the woken code reconfigures the clock and power settings. During sleep mode the CPU clock is gated to conserve power, and all register contents and the program counter are retained. If the clock source for MCLK is disabled during sleep, an enabled interrupt powers up and enables the source clock for the duration of interrupt servicing.

Clock and power management, including sleep mode configuration, are controlled through the \peripheral{SYSTEM} peripheral (Section~\ref{ss:sleep}). If SMCLK is disabled, peripherals in the SMCLK domain cannot assert their interrupts and cannot wake the CPU.

\clearpage



% The per-class cycle costs, the straddling-fetch residual and the benchmark CPI in
% this chapter are measured on the RTL (GHDL, bare core, single hart out of TCM), not
% derived. Every figure printed here is recorded in verification/cpi/expected.json and
% gated by //verification/cpi: a core change that moves CPI turns that gate red until
% the numbers here move with it.
\chapter{Core performance and instruction timing} \label{s:cpi}

The VestaRV core is a multi-cycle machine on a single unified instruction and data bus, but it issues the fetch of the next instruction during the execute cycle of the current one. Most instructions therefore retire at one per MCLK cycle, and the core's measured cycles-per-instruction (CPI) is much closer to 1 than the term ``multi-cycle'' on its own would suggest: over the benchmark suite of Section~\ref{ss:cpi-measured} it is 1.260. This chapter gives the cost of every instruction class and reports the CPI measured on that suite.

Every figure below is for one hart executing out of its own TCM with no shared-bus contention. An access that crosses the arbiter into the shared window, or that is made while another hart holds the grant, adds stall cycles on top of these numbers (Chapter~\ref{s:multicore}). The core's clock is gated while it waits, so a stalled cycle is still an MCLK cycle in which nothing retires and it is charged to CPI like any other.

\section{Instruction timing} \label{ss:cpi-timing}

Table~\ref{t:cpi-timing} gives the cost of each instruction class. A row for an optional extension applies only when that extension is configured for this build; a disabled extension's instructions raise an illegal-instruction trap instead of executing. Atomic memory operations are the one class not re-measured here, because the bare-core bench has no second master; their 5-cycle cost is the design value.

\begin{longtable}[c]{ l l }
\caption{Measured instruction timing, in MCLK cycles.} \label{t:cpi-timing} \\
\hline \textbf{Instruction class} & \textbf{MCLK cycles} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Instruction class} & \textbf{MCLK cycles} \\ \hline \endhead
                               Arithmetic and logical (\asminline{add}, \asminline{andi}, \asminline{lui}, \asminline{auipc}) & 1 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} Shift (\asminline{sll}, \asminline{srl}, \asminline{sra} and immediate forms) & 1 \\
                               Comparison (\asminline{slt}, \asminline{sltu} and immediate forms) & 1 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} Bit manipulation (Zba, Zbb, Zbc, Zbs) & 1 \\
                               Multiply (M): \asminline{mul}, \asminline{mulh}, \asminline{mulhu}, \asminline{mulhsu} & 1 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} Divide and remainder (M): \asminline{div}, \asminline{divu}, \asminline{rem}, \asminline{remu} & 36 \\
                               Load and store (\asminline{lw}, \asminline{lh}, \asminline{lb}, \asminline{sw}, \asminline{sh}, \asminline{sb}) & 2 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} Conditional branch, whether taken or not taken & 1 \\
                               Jump and link (\asminline{jal}, \asminline{jalr}) & 1 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} CSR read (\asminline{csrr}) & 1 \\
                               Atomic memory operations (A) & 5 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \emph{Additional} penalty: 32-bit instruction straddling a word boundary, reached sequentially & 0 \\
                               \emph{Additional} penalty: the same, reached by a taken branch or jump & +1 \\
\hline
\end{longtable}

Three entries are worth drawing out. Hardware multiply is single-cycle, so \asminline{mul} costs no more than \asminline{add} and there is no reason to hand-expand a multiplication into shifts and adds. Divide and remainder share one iterative divider and are, by a wide margin, the most expensive instructions the core executes; where the divisor is a constant, the compiler's multiply-and-shift expansion is far faster than \asminline{div} and is worth checking for in the disassembly of any hot loop. And a conditional branch costs the same whether it is taken or not, because the core resolves the condition and issues the redirected fetch in the same cycle: there is no branch predictor, and no misprediction penalty to design around.

The two straddling rows are one instruction class split by how the core arrives at it, and Section~\ref{ss:cpi-align} is about that split.

\section{Compressed instructions and fetch alignment} \label{ss:cpi-align}

The core fetches one 32-bit word per bus cycle. With the C extension enabled instructions are only guaranteed 2-byte aligned, so a 32-bit instruction may straddle a word boundary, and the core must have both halves before it can decode. Compressed (2-byte) instructions and word-aligned 32-bit instructions are never affected.

The core covers most of that case in hardware, with a fetch-ahead. When it is about to step sequentially onto a straddling 32-bit instruction, it can already see that instruction's lower half in the word it is holding, and the fetch its ordinary sequencing would issue is for the word it is holding already, a bus cycle that would carry nothing new. The fetch-ahead spends that cycle on the next word instead and latches the lower half at the same edge, so the straddling instruction dispatches in one cycle and costs nothing at all. The whole mechanism is one flip-flop, it issues no bus cycle the core would not have issued one cycle later, and it changes cycle counts only, never an architectural result. It is the \texttt{core.fetchAhead} knob of Table~\ref{t:chip-config} (the \texttt{ENABLE\_IF\_AHEAD} generic on the core), it is on in this build, and turning it off is a performance choice and nothing else.

What the fetch-ahead cannot cover is a taken control transfer whose target is a half-word-aligned 32-bit instruction. It arms only on a sequential advance, because that is the only case in which the core can prove, from a half-word it can already see, what it is about to fetch; after a taken branch or jump the core arrives at the target holding nothing, and genuinely needs two fetches before it can decode. That case still costs one extra cycle, and it is the whole of the residual reported below. Both rows of Table~\ref{t:cpi-timing} are measured directly: a straight-line block in which every 32-bit instruction straddles runs at 1.000 cycles per instruction, while a block of a taken branch, a straddling 32-bit target and a compressed instruction (three instructions that cost one cycle each on their own) takes 4 cycles.

Table~\ref{t:cpi-align} isolates what the C extension still costs by rebuilding the whole benchmark suite for RV32IMA instead of RV32IMAC. The compiler emits the identical instruction sequence in both builds (the retired-instruction counts match exactly, benchmark for benchmark) and only the encoding differs, so the entire difference in cycle count is the straddling-fetch penalty that survives the fetch-ahead. Across the suite it is 0.031 CPI, or 2.2\% of all cycles.

\begin{longtable}[c]{ l r r r r }
\caption{Straddling fetches that survive the fetch-ahead, measured with and without the C extension.} \label{t:cpi-align} \\
\hline \textbf{Benchmark} & \textbf{CPI (RV32IMAC)} & \textbf{CPI (RV32IMA)} & \textbf{Penalty, CPI} & \textbf{Cycles lost} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Benchmark} & \textbf{CPI (RV32IMAC)} & \textbf{CPI (RV32IMA)} & \textbf{Penalty, CPI} & \textbf{Cycles lost} \\ \hline \endhead
                               \texttt{dhrystone} & 1.504 & 1.481 & 0.022 & 1.5\% \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{median}    & 1.398 & 1.397 & 0.000 & 0.0\% \\
                               \texttt{memcpy}    & 1.726 & 1.726 & 0.000 & 0.0\% \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{multiply}  & 1.163 & 1.014 & 0.148 & 12.8\% \\
                               \texttt{qsort}     & 1.398 & 1.330 & 0.068 & 4.8\% \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{rsort}     & 1.412 & 1.412 & 0.000 & 0.0\% \\
                               \texttt{towers}    & 1.682 & 1.681 & 0.002 & 0.1\% \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{vvadd}     & 1.374 & 1.374 & 0.000 & 0.0\% \\
\hline
                               \textbf{Aggregate} & \textbf{1.443} & \textbf{1.412} & \textbf{0.031} & \textbf{2.2\%} \\
\hline
\end{longtable}

The aggregate row weights each benchmark by its retired-instruction count, and covers the eight benchmarks of Table~\ref{t:cpi-bench} that were rebuilt both ways; \texttt{spmv} was not, which is why this aggregate differs from the one in that table.

Four of the eight benchmarks pay nothing measurable: their straddling instructions are all reached sequentially, and the hardware absorbs every one. What is left is concentrated in short, branch-dense loops, and \texttt{multiply} is the extreme case: its inner loop is seven instructions long and, in the measured build, its head is a half-word-aligned 32-bit \asminline{and}, so the loop's own backward branch lands on a straddling instruction on every iteration, and one loop head accounts for the entire 12.8\%.

That is the whole of the alignment advice. Aligning a hot loop's body buys nothing: the fetch-ahead already covers straight-line code, and a body of compressed instructions never straddled in the first place. What still pays is aligning branch targets: loop heads, and the entry of a hot function reached by a call. In C, \texttt{-falign-loops=4} does exactly that across a translation unit, and it complements hand alignment rather than replacing it: rebuilding \texttt{multiply} with it moves that one loop head onto a word boundary and recovers the entire residual, bringing the benchmark back to the RV32IMA figure in the table above, while an assembly hot spot or a computed jump target is aligned by hand with \asminline{.p2align 2} on the label. None of this is an argument against the C extension, which is configured on by default and earns its place by shrinking code substantially, decisive when a hart's private TCM is \TcmSizeKiB{} KiB.

\section{Measured CPI} \label{ss:cpi-measured}

Table~\ref{t:cpi-bench} reports CPI over nine benchmarks derived from the riscv-tests benchmark suite, compiled \texttt{-O2} for RV32IMAC with the Zb* extensions enabled. The measured region is each benchmark's own timed kernel, so it excludes program startup, the cache-warming pass, and result verification.

\begin{longtable}[c]{ l r r }
\caption{Measured CPI by benchmark (timed kernel, single hart, no bus contention).} \label{t:cpi-bench} \\
\hline \textbf{Benchmark} & \textbf{Instructions retired} & \textbf{CPI} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Benchmark} & \textbf{Instructions retired} & \textbf{CPI} \\ \hline \endhead
                               \texttt{spmv}      & 802{,}447 & 1.143 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{multiply}  & 20{,}892  & 1.163 \\
                               \texttt{vvadd}     & 2{,}408   & 1.374 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{median}    & 4{,}015   & 1.398 \\
                               \texttt{qsort}     & 123{,}205 & 1.398 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{rsort}     & 146{,}548 & 1.412 \\
                               \texttt{dhrystone} & 200{,}523 & 1.504 \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{towers}    & 3{,}747   & 1.682 \\
                               \texttt{memcpy}    & 11{,}017  & 1.726 \\
\hline
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \textbf{Aggregate} & \textbf{1{,}314{,}802} & \textbf{1.260} \\
\hline
\end{longtable}

The aggregate is the total cycle count over the total retired-instruction count, so each benchmark contributes in proportion to the work it does. Read against Table~\ref{t:cpi-timing}, the spread has a simple explanation: the further a workload sits above 1.0, the more of its instruction mix is loads and stores, which cost two cycles each on the unified bus. Fetch alignment barely enters into it: \texttt{multiply} is register-bound and runs at 1.163, of which 0.148 is the one unaligned loop head of Section~\ref{ss:cpi-align} and the rest is its own work, and \texttt{towers} and \texttt{memcpy} sit at the other end because they are dominated by memory traffic. Branches move none of it, since they are free.

\section{Measuring application code} \label{ss:cpi-measure}

The core implements the \register{cycle}/\register{cycleh} and \register{instret}/\register{instreth} counters, and their machine-mode aliases \register{mcycle} and \register{minstret}, in every configuration. \register{cycle} counts MCLK cycles, free-running and independent of whether the core is stalled; \register{minstret} counts instructions actually retired. Bracketing a region with \asminline{rdcycle} and \asminline{rdinstret} and taking the differences therefore gives that region's exact cycle count and CPI on hardware, with no external instrumentation:

\begin{lstlisting}[style=customC]
unsigned c0, i0, c1, i1;
__asm__ volatile ("rdcycle %0; rdinstret %1" : "=r"(c0), "=r"(i0));
hot_loop();
__asm__ volatile ("rdcycle %0; rdinstret %1" : "=r"(c1), "=r"(i1));
/* cycles = c1 - c0, instructions = i1 - i0 */
\end{lstlisting}

\register{time} and \register{timeh} are not implemented in any configuration, because no real-time source is wired to the core, and reading either raises an illegal-instruction trap. Use \register{cycle} for elapsed time, converting through the known MCLK frequency, or a timer peripheral for wall-clock measurement.

\section{Measurement methodology} \label{ss:cpi-method}

The numbers in this chapter are measured on the RTL, not estimated. Each benchmark is run to completion in a VHDL simulation of the bare core with a one-cycle-latency memory and no bus back-pressure, which is the timing a single hart sees executing from its own TCM. Cycles are counted on the free-running core clock, so any cycle in which the core's clock is gated is still counted. Instructions are counted from the core's internal instruction-retire strobe, the same signal that increments \register{minstret}, so the instruction count is architectural rather than an estimate derived from the simulation. The core under measurement is configured as this build ships it, fetch-ahead included.

The per-class costs in Table~\ref{t:cpi-timing} come from paired micro-kernels: a loop containing 64 copies of the instruction under test is run against an otherwise identical empty loop, and the difference in cycles divided by the difference in retired instructions gives the marginal cost of that instruction alone, with the loop's own overhead subtracted out. Every micro-kernel body is word-aligned, so no class is charged a fetch cost that is not its own, with two deliberate exceptions: the two kernels that measure the straddling rows are built to straddle. One is a straight-line block of four instructions, two of them straddling 32-bit ones and every one of them reached sequentially, which measures 1.000 cycles per instruction; the other is a taken branch onto a straddling 32-bit target followed by a compressed instruction, three instructions whose measured classes cost one cycle each, which measures 4 cycles for the block.

\part{Boot ROM and software}

\chapter{ROM monitor} \label{s:forth}

When the chip leaves reset with the \pin{P0.7} strap low (Section~\ref{ss:bootmode}), hart 0 runs the ROM monitor: an interactive Forth interpreter stored in the boot ROM that communicates over \peripheral{UART0} at 115,200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit. The monitor is a bring-up console and the flash programming path of Chapter~\ref{s:programming}; it is not a development environment.

% The banner is printed by software/bootrom_mp/src/rv4th.c as ASIC_NAME " rv4th-rom!",
% with ASIC_NAME from software/commune/include/myshkin.h. Its leading word is the name
% compiled into that header, not this chip's name, so the manual does not quote it.
On start-up the monitor prints a one-line banner ending in \forthinline{rv4th-rom!}, an empty line, and the prompt \forthinline{>}, and is then ready to receive characters. The leading word of the banner is the \texttt{ASIC\_NAME} string compiled into the ROM source and does not name this chip.

\section{Interpreter model}

Forth is a stack language. Every value is a 32-bit signed integer on one data stack, the top of which is called TOS. Typing a number pushes it: a plain decimal integer, or a hexadecimal value with the prefix \forthinline{0x} in either case and without leading zeros (\forthinline{0xA4}). Typing a word (a function name) executes it; a word pops its arguments from the stack and pushes its results. Nothing is executed until a line feed is received, at which point the whole line is executed left to right. An input the interpreter does not recognise as a number or a word prints \forthinline{?}. Stack underflow is not an error: a pop from an empty stack yields 0.

By default the monitor echoes every received character back to the host, which suits a terminal emulator; \forthinline{0 echo} switches the echo off for a programmatic host.

\section{Word list}

The words below are listed with their stack effect in the usual Forth notation: the items left of the double dash are the arguments as they are typed (the rightmost is the TOS when the word runs), and the items right of it are the results, rightmost on top. Arguments are popped before the word executes and results are pushed after it finishes.

\input{include/ForthCommandsItemized.tex}

\section{Interpreter limits} \label{ss:forthlimits}

The interpreter keeps all of its mutable state in hart 0's TCM, of which the interrupt vector table takes the first \VectorsCount{} words and the top 1 KiB is reserved for the C stack; the interpreter's arrays are sized to what is left. The capacities are fixed by the ROM and are not configurable at run time:

\begin{itemize}[itemsep=1pt]
	\item Data (math) stack: 128 cells of 32 bits.
	\item Return (address) stack: 64 cells of 32 bits. Each active \forthinline{do loop} uses three of them, so loop nesting is bounded well below that.
	\item Dictionary: 64 user-defined words, 512 bytes total of word names including the separating space after each, and 1024 opcodes of compiled body shared by all of them.
	\item Input line buffer: 128 characters.
	\item Word buffer: 64 characters, so a single word name is at most 63 characters.
\end{itemize}

Only three of these are checked at run time: math stack underflow, input line overflow and word buffer overflow. Exceeding the dictionary capacities or underflowing the return stack is not detected and corrupts interpreter state. A program that outgrows these limits belongs in the SPI flash boot mode of Chapter~\ref{s:programming}.

\begin{Caution}
The monitor's receive path is a polled loop with no flow control, and it echoes each character as it takes it. A host that delivers a line back to back at 115,200 baud can lose characters; a host that leaves one character time of idle line between frames does not.
\end{Caution}

\section{Defining words}

A new word is defined with \forthinline{: name body ;}, where \forthinline{body} is any sequence of numbers and words. The new word may be used as soon as the semicolon has been read, even later on the same line. A user-defined word can only push and pop the stack and call other words. For example, a word that increments the TOS:

\noindent\forthinlinehl{: inc 1 + ;}

\section{Conditionals}

\forthinline{if} and \forthinline{then} form a conditional and may only be used inside a word definition. \forthinline{if} pops the TOS and executes the words up to the matching \forthinline{then} only when the popped value is nonzero. An \forthinline{else} clause is optional:

\noindent\forthinlinehl{cond if wordsIfTrue else wordsIfFalse then}

\noindent For example, a word that prints \forthinline{cool} when the TOS equals 5:

\noindent\forthinlinehl{: cool? 5 == if 108 111 111 99 emit emit emit emit then ;}

\section{Loops}

Two loop forms exist, and both may only be used inside a word definition. \forthinline{begin ... until} executes its body, then pops the TOS at \forthinline{until} and repeats the body while the popped value is zero. \forthinline{stop start do ... loop} is a counted loop: it runs its body with the index taking the values \forthinline{start} to \forthinline{stop - 1}. Inside a counted loop the word \forthinline{i} pushes the index of the innermost loop, and \forthinline{j} and \forthinline{k} the indices of the two enclosing loops. For example, a word that prints the numbers 0 to 9:

\noindent\forthinlinehl{: looptest 10 0 do i . loop ;}

\clearpage



\chapter{Boot image format} \label{s:programming}

% Source of every address in this chapter: software/bootrom_mp/src/start.S
% (spi_flash_boot, getCommandWord, loadSegmentToRAM, eraseSegmentFromRAM,
% executeProgram and the BOOT_ENTRY_VEC dispatch), software/commune/include/
% myshkin_s.h (PROG_BASE_ADDR 0x8200, BOOT_ENTRY_VEC 0x10640, RAM_SIZE) and
% verification/isa/flash_prepend.sh. The generated define \SpiFlashProgramAddress
% (0x8200) is the RAM entry address, not a flash address: the ROM reads the flash
% from offset 0.
When the \pin{P0.7} strap is high at reset (Section~\ref{ss:bootmode}), hart 0's boot loader reads a boot image from the SPI flash on \peripheral{SPI0}, copies its segments into RAM and enters it. The image is a stream of 32-bit words beginning at flash offset \texttt{0x000000}, read with one continuous high-frequency read command. Table~\ref{t:boot-image} is the authoritative description of the stream.

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l p{4.4cm} X}
\caption{Boot image stream, as read by the boot ROM from flash offset \texttt{0x000000}.} \label{t:boot-image} \\
\hline \textbf{Command word} & \textbf{Following words} & \textbf{Effect} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Command word} & \textbf{Following words} & \textbf{Effect} \\ \hline \endhead
\texttt{0x10ADBEEF} & \texttt{START}, \texttt{END}, then $(\mathtt{END}-\mathtt{START})/4$ data words & Load segment: the data words are stored to RAM at \texttt{START}, \texttt{START + 4}, \dots, \texttt{END - 4}. \texttt{END} is exclusive. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{0xDEADBEEF} & \texttt{START}, \texttt{END}, \texttt{VALUE} & Fill segment: every word from \texttt{START} to \texttt{END - 4} is set to \texttt{VALUE}. \\
\texttt{0xCAFEBABE} & none & Execute: the loader ends the flash read, restores the \peripheral{SPI0} pins, selects the boot clocks, clears the registers and enters the image. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

Every segment must lie inside the load window: \texttt{\RamStartAddress} $\le$ \texttt{START} $<$ \texttt{END} $\le$ \texttt{\SharedRamEndAddress} + 1, which spans the private TCM, the NPU staging RAM and the shared RAM. A segment outside the window, or any other command word, traps the boot loader. The entry address is the word at \texttt{0x10640} in shared RAM if the image has loaded a nonzero value there, and \texttt{\SpiFlashProgramAddress} otherwise; the loader zeroes the shared-RAM mailbox region before reading the flash, so an image that publishes nothing enters at \texttt{\SpiFlashProgramAddress}.

Words are transferred most-significant byte first: the flash byte at offset $4k$ is bits 31:24 of word $k$. A tool that writes the flash from a little-endian memory image must therefore reverse the byte order within every word.

A standard image, as produced by the build scripts, consists of a fill or load segment that zeroes the vector table region \texttt{\RamStartAddress} to \texttt{\SpiFlashProgramAddress}, one load segment per contiguous run of nonzero program words (a run of eight or more zero words separates segments, and each segment is padded by two trailing zero words), and the execute word. The image's first instruction is at \texttt{\SpiFlashProgramAddress} in the TCM unless it publishes an entry address; an image larger than the TCM executes from the shared RAM and publishes its entry there. The vector table itself is written by the image's startup code.

\section{Programming the flash from the ROM monitor} \label{ss:flashprog}

The ROM monitor (Chapter~\ref{s:forth}) writes, erases and reads the flash in 256-byte pages, and \texttt{tools/flash\_programmer/forthprog.py} in the repository (Appendix~\ref{s:software}) drives it to program a whole image from an Intel hex file. The image occupies flash pages from offset \texttt{0x000000} upward, as many as its length requires.

\begin{description}[style=nextline, leftmargin=0pt, itemsep=2pt]
	\item[\texttt{bin addr fw}] Writes one page at flash address \forthinline{addr}, which must be a multiple of 256. If \forthinline{bin} is nonzero the monitor expects 256 bytes of binary data; if zero, a 512-character ASCII hex string. After the line feed the monitor prints \forthinline{\$} when it is ready for the data. When the data has arrived it prints the CRC of the page as four hex characters (CRC16/CDMA2000: polynomial \texttt{0xC857}, initial value \texttt{0xFFFF}, no final XOR, no reflection). The host answers with a single \forthinline{Y} to commit the write; any other character aborts it and leaves the flash unchanged.
	\item[\texttt{conf addr fe}] Erases the page at \forthinline{addr} to \texttt{0xFF} when \forthinline{conf} equals 123 and pushes 1; otherwise does nothing and pushes 0. Erasing is faster than writing and is the right way to handle a blank page.
	\item[\texttt{fr}] Reads the flash back; see Section~\ref{ss:forthflash}.
\end{description}

\begin{Note}
The flash device specifies a page program time of up to 25 ms (typically 10 ms) and a page erase time of up to 25 ms (typically 6 ms). The handshake of \forthinline{fw} is long enough that no extra delay is needed between writes; consecutive erases at a high baud rate may need one.
\end{Note}

After the image is written, the chip runs it after a reset with the \pin{P0.7} strap high. The \forthinline{rst} word restarts hart 0 at the boot ROM without a pin reset, so a host that controls the strap can switch modes without toggling \pin{RESETN}.

\clearpage



\appendix

\chapter{Getting started and software development} \label{s:software}

The RTL of this chip, its boot ROM, its firmware applications, the generated headers and this manual are one repository, \url{https://github.com/maxxseminario/VestaRV}. Every command in this appendix is run from the root of a clone of it and needs nothing installed first: the build provisions its own Python, its host and RISC-V compilers, its VHDL simulator and its \TeX{} distribution. Synthesis, place-and-route and physical signoff run on licensed tools that are not part of the repository and are not described here.

\section{First run} \label{ss:swfirstrun}

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
	\item Clone the repository.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
git clone https://github.com/maxxseminario/VestaRV.git
cd VestaRV
\end{lstlisting}
	\item Fetch the build driver. The script writes one launcher, \texttt{tools/bin/bazel}, and touches nothing outside the clone.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
sh tools/get_bazel.sh
\end{lstlisting}
	\item Run the gate set.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
tools/bin/bazel test //...
\end{lstlisting}
	That is 337 tests: the generated RTL against the tracked RTL, the register descriptions against both the VHDL and the C headers, every firmware image against its tracked golden, and a license-free simulation regression of the instruction set. The first run fetches about 1 GB of toolchains and builds the VHDL simulator from source, 10 to 20 minutes; every later run is served from the cache.
	\item Emit the artifacts of this configuration.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
make -C platform/common generate
\end{lstlisting}
	The run writes the RTL to \texttt{platform/common/out/hdl/}, the C headers to \texttt{out/software/include/}, the linker script fragments to \texttt{out/linker-scripts/}, the pad ring to \texttt{out/config/PadRing.json} and the sources of this manual to \texttt{platform/common/latex/TRM/}. \bashinline{CONFIG=config/<name>.json} selects another configuration. The hermetic equivalent, which writes only into \texttt{bazel-bin}, is \bashinline{tools/bin/bazel build //platform/common:chip_artifacts_<name>}, one target per tracked configuration.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent Table~\ref{t:sw-toolchain} lists what the build fetches. None of it is installed on the host, and none of it has to be on \texttt{PATH}.

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{p{4.4cm} X}
\caption{Tools the build provisions on first use.} \label{t:sw-toolchain} \\
\hline \textbf{Tool} & \textbf{Version and origin} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Tool} & \textbf{Version and origin} \\ \hline \endhead
RISC-V C compiler & \texttt{riscv-none-elf-gcc} 13.2.0, fetched and hash-pinned in \texttt{MODULE.bazel}. The mask-ROM image has to reproduce byte for byte, so this compiler is never substituted. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} Build driver & Bazel 9.2.0, run through the \texttt{bazelisk} launcher that \texttt{tools/get\_bazel.sh} installs. \\
Python & 3.11, provisioned by \texttt{rules\_python} for every generator and test. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} Host C/C++ compiler & Hermetic \texttt{zig}-based toolchain, so a host with no system compiler still builds. \\
VHDL simulator & GHDL 6.0.0, built from source with the mcode backend. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \TeX{} & TeX Live 2022, for this manual. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

\section{Building a firmware image} \label{ss:swimages}

Every application under \texttt{software/} is built by one macro, \texttt{myshkin\_app} in \texttt{toolchains/riscv/defs.bzl}: the sources are compiled \bashinline{-march=rv32ima -mabi=ilp32 -O2}, linked against \texttt{tools/build/linker-scripts/MCU.ld} and the generated memory-map fragments, and imaged. One application builds the whole artifact set of Table~\ref{t:sw-artifacts}.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
tools/bin/bazel build //software/blinky:blinky_flashed_rcf
tools/bin/bazel build //software/...
tools/bin/bazel build //software/bootrom_mp:rom_rcf
\end{lstlisting}

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{p{4.4cm} X}
\caption{Artifacts of one firmware target, for a package \texttt{//software/NAME}.} \label{t:sw-artifacts} \\
\hline \textbf{Target} & \textbf{What it is} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Target} & \textbf{What it is} \\ \hline \endhead
\texttt{:NAME\_elf} & Linked ELF with debug symbols, and the map file beside it. The file a debugger loads. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{:NAME\_bin} & Raw binary of the loaded image. \\
\texttt{:NAME\_hex} & Intel hex image, the input to the flash programmer of Section~\ref{ss:swload}. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{:NAME\_dump} & Disassembly listing. \\
\texttt{:NAME\_rcf} & One 32-bit word of the RAM image per line, for the VHDL benches. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{:NAME\_flashed\_rcf} & The same image as the boot-image stream of Chapter~\ref{s:programming}, command words and all, ready for the SPI flash. \\
\texttt{:NAME\_flashed\_rcf\_test} & Gate: the built image is byte-identical to the tracked golden under \texttt{NAME/testdata/}. A firmware change is committed with its regenerated golden, so the diff shows which bytes moved. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

\noindent The applications in the repository are \texttt{blinky} (\peripheral{TIMER0} drives \pin{P3.0} at 1 Hz with no processor in the loop), \texttt{gpiotoggle} (the same pad toggled from a CPU loop), \texttt{slowblink} (a CPU delay loop at a human-visible rate), \texttt{looptest} (an infinite loop that traps on nothing, which is how a load that worked is told from one that did not) and \texttt{traptest} (an all-zeros word, which traps). \texttt{//software/bootrom\_mp:rom\_rcf} is the mask-ROM content of the fabricated part; \texttt{:rom\_rcf\_reproducibility\_test} is the gate that it cannot drift.

\section{A program of your own} \label{ss:swnew}

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
	\item Create the package and take the startup file from an existing one.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
mkdir -p software/myapp/src
cp software/blinky/src/start.S software/myapp/src/start.S
\end{lstlisting}
	\texttt{start.S} must be the first source in link order: the linker script places its first instruction at \texttt{\SpiFlashProgramAddress}, the address the boot loader enters (Chapter~\ref{s:programming}). It sets the stack pointer, clears \texttt{.bss} and calls \texttt{main}.
	\item Write \texttt{src/main.c} against the generated headers. \texttt{software/include/regs/} holds one header per peripheral block, emitted from the SystemRDL descriptions in \texttt{hdl/common/regs/rdl/}, and \texttt{castalia\_regs.h} includes all of them and adds, for each instance of this build, a base address \texttt{<INST>\_BASE\_ADDR}, a typed pointer \texttt{<INST>\_REGS} and, where the instance owns one, an interrupt vector \texttt{<INST>\_IRQ\_VECTOR}. Within a block the names are \texttt{<REG>\_T\_\_<FIELD>\_bm} for the mask, \texttt{\_bp} for the position, \texttt{\_bw} for the width, \texttt{\_reset} for the reset value, and \texttt{<REG>\_T\_\_<FIELD>\_\_<VALUE>} for an enumerated field value. Every number in Part~III is in these headers under those names.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=C]
#include "castalia_regs.h"

#define HFXT_HZ   24000000u
#define BAUD      115200u

static void uart0_putc(char c)
{
    while (UART0_REGS->UARTxSR & UARTXSR_T__TXBF_bm) { }
    UART0_REGS->UARTxTX = (uint8_t)c;
}

int main(void)
{
    SYSTEM_REGS->SYSCLKCR =
        (SYSCLKCR_T__MCLKSEL__HFXT  << SYSCLKCR_T__MCLKSEL_bp) |
        (SYSCLKCR_T__SMCLKSEL__HFXT << SYSCLKCR_T__SMCLKSEL_bp);

    UART0_REGS->UARTxBR = (HFXT_HZ / (16u * BAUD)) - 1u;
    UART0_REGS->UARTxCR = UARTXCR_T__UEN_bm;

    GPIO2_REGS->PxSEL = 0x00;
    GPIO2_REGS->PxDIR = 0x01;

    for (;;) {
        uart0_putc('.');
        GPIO2_REGS->PxOUTT = 0x01;
    }
    return 0;
}
\end{lstlisting}
	The block struct carries the template spelling of the register, not the instance spelling: the instance is in the pointer, so \texttt{UART0\_REGS->UARTxCR} is \peripheral{UART0}'s control register. The boot ROM leaves the clock system in a state of its own (Section~\ref{ss:bootmode}), which is why the first write selects the SMCLK source before the baud divider is programmed. The \pin{TX0} pad is already at its alternate function after reset (Table~\ref{t:gpio-pins}), so the program configures no pin for the UART and only the GPIO pad it drives itself.
	\item Add \texttt{software/myapp/BUILD.bazel}. The \texttt{hdrs} and \texttt{copts} lines are what put the generated headers inside the sandbox; without them the build fails rather than silently compiling against a stale copy.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
load("//toolchains/riscv:defs.bzl", "myshkin_app")

package(default_visibility = ["//visibility:public"])

myshkin_app(
    name = "myapp",
    copts = ["-Isoftware/include/regs"],
    hdrs = ["//software/include:regs_headers"],
)
\end{lstlisting}
	\item Build the image.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
tools/bin/bazel build //software/myapp:myapp_flashed_rcf
\end{lstlisting}
	\item Lock it against drift by adding a \texttt{firmware\_image\_test} beside the application, as \texttt{software/blinky/BUILD.bazel} does, and committing the golden it grades.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent \texttt{myshkin\_app} compiles for \texttt{rv32ima}, which harts 1 to \MaxHartIndex{} do not implement: this build's tiles are \texttt{rv32iac} (Section~\ref{ss:isa}), and the multiply instructions trap there. An image that runs on a tile is built with \texttt{rv32\_firmware} directly and \bashinline{march = "rv32iac"}, which is the same macro one level down with every flag exposed.

\section{Simulating the image before silicon} \label{ss:swsim}

The simulation tier needs no license: the simulator is built from source by the same command that runs the test. Table~\ref{t:sw-sim} lists the targets.

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{p{6.2cm} X}
\caption{Simulation targets, all license-free.} \label{t:sw-sim} \\
\hline \textbf{Target} & \textbf{What it proves} \\ \hline \endfirsthead
\hline \textbf{Target} & \textbf{What it proves} \\ \hline \endhead
\texttt{//opensource\_sim:isa\_regression} & The whole nine-suite instruction-set regression on the core. Run it after any change to the core or to the extensions a program compiles for. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{//opensource\_sim/isa:} \texttt{rv32ui-p-add} & One image on the bare-core bench, which is the per-image debug loop. That bench is one hart, one flat RAM at \texttt{\RamStartAddress} and no peripherals, so an image of your own runs there only if it touches no peripheral window; the rule to copy is the \texttt{ghdl\_test} in \texttt{opensource\_sim/isa/BUILD.bazel}, with \texttt{image} naming your \texttt{:NAME\_rcf}. \\
\texttt{//opensource\_sim/asic\_default:} \texttt{asic\_default\_elaborate} & The generated MCU binds and its memory-size assertions hold. \\
\rowcolor{tablehighlightcolor} \texttt{//opensource\_sim/asic\_default:} \texttt{asic\_default\_boot} & Reset is released on the real mask-ROM image and the banner the ROM monitor prints on \peripheral{UART0} is graded. It proves the part fetched through the arbiter, ran C out of its TCM and drove a pad. \\
\texttt{//opensource\_sim/rv4th:} \texttt{rv4th\_forth} & The ROM monitor answers its own bench over \peripheral{UART0}, word by word. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

\section{Loading a program onto a chip} \label{ss:swload}

Both host paths talk to the ROM monitor (Chapter~\ref{s:forth}) over \peripheral{UART0} at 115,200 baud, 8N1, with the \pin{P0.7} strap low at reset (Section~\ref{ss:bootmode}). The scripts are in \texttt{tools/flash\_programmer/} and need \texttt{pyserial}; \texttt{forthprog.py} also needs \texttt{IntelHex} and \texttt{progressbar2}.

\paragraph{Into the SPI flash, which survives a power cycle.} Program the flash through the monitor, then strap \pin{P0.7} high and reset. The boot loader reads the image from flash offset \texttt{0x000000}, copies its segments into RAM and enters it (Chapter~\ref{s:programming}). The monitor's \forthinline{rst} word restarts hart 0 without a pin reset, so a host that controls the strap needs no power cycle.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
python3 tools/flash_programmer/forthprog.py -p /dev/ttyUSB0 -v \
    bazel-bin/software/myapp/myapp.hex
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{Straight into RAM, which does not touch the flash.} The image is written word by word through the monitor's memory-write word and entered with \forthinline{call0}. This is the path when the flash is unpopulated or its boot path is under suspicion, and it is the faster edit-and-run loop. The image's basename is padded with leading \texttt{x} to 22 characters, which is a fixed-length path contract of the VHDL benches and not a typing error.

\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
python3 tools/flash_programmer/forthram.py -p /dev/ttyUSB0 --verify \
    bazel-bin/software/myapp/xxxxxxxxxxxxxmyapp.rcf
\end{lstlisting}

\noindent \texttt{rcf2forth.py} turns either image into a plain list of monitor commands with no hardware attached, \texttt{forthrun.py} streams such a list, and \texttt{tools/debug/rv4th\_terminal.py} is an interactive terminal on the same port. The page-write handshake and the flash words those scripts drive are described in Section~\ref{ss:flashprog}.

\section{Debugging on the part} \label{ss:swdebug}

The debug port is a 5-pin JTAG TAP in front of a RISC-V Debug Module; Chapter~\ref{s:debug} is the reference and Section~\ref{ss:debug-limits} is the list of behaviours that will surprise a debugger. The part has been brought up against unmodified OpenOCD 0.12.0 and \texttt{riscv-none-elf-gdb} 13.2, which are host tools and are not provisioned by the build.

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
	\item Start OpenOCD on \texttt{tools/debug/riscv-tests-debug/targets/VestaRV/} \texttt{vesta\_castalia.cfg}. It declares the TAP (IDCODE \texttt{0x1CA57EEF}, 5-bit IR), creates one target per hart, and forces every memory access through the program buffer, which is required because the module implements no system bus access. The file's transport lines drive a simulation bridge; on silicon replace them with the adapter's own driver and \bashinline{adapter speed 3000} or slower, for the reason in Section~\ref{ss:debug-limits}.
	\item Attach the debugger to the port OpenOCD reports, and raise its timeout: a memory read through the program buffer is far slower than the 2-second default assumes.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
riscv-none-elf-gdb bazel-bin/software/myapp/myapp.elf
(gdb) set remotetimeout 120
(gdb) target extended-remote localhost:3333
\end{lstlisting}
	\item Halt, step, read state, resume. Registers follow the selected thread; memory follows the connection's target, which is hart 0, so per-tile memory work uses the independent-target configuration \texttt{vesta\_castalia\_nosmp.cfg} and one debugger per hart.
\begin{lstlisting}[language=bash]
(gdb) monitor halt
(gdb) info registers pc mstatus mcause
(gdb) x/8xw 0x10640
(gdb) stepi
(gdb) continue
\end{lstlisting}
	\item Set breakpoints with \texttt{break}, never \texttt{hbreak}: there are no hardware triggers, so a breakpoint is an \asminline{EBREAK} written over the instruction and cannot be placed in the boot ROM or any other read-only region.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent A program image cannot be loaded over the debug port. \register{abstractauto} is unimplemented, so a burst write lands only its first word; use the ROM monitor of Section~\ref{ss:swload} to load, and the debug port to inspect.
